name: Energy distribution
summary: Only some particles reach the energy source; particles must share energy so that every action is paid for.
statement: Each action costs energy, and only $s$ particles, the **sources**, can harvest energy from outside. Particles must distribute energy locally so that every particle can act, or so that a given energy-agnostic algorithm runs correctly. **Time** is in rounds.

primer.intro: Think of a colony of bacteria where only cells at the edge of the colony get food and must pass nutrients inward so that every cell can keep working. The floor is the **triangular lattice**: the endless graph whose **nodes** are the corners of a tiling of the plane by equal triangles; each node is joined by an edge to six others, its **neighbours**. A **particle** occupies one node and moves in two actions: an **expansion** into an empty neighbouring node, after which it occupies both, then a **contraction** into one of the two; so one expansion and one contraction move it by one node. The **system** of $n$ particles is connected; only $s$ of them, the **sources**, can take energy from outside. Every action (a move, or any step of some other algorithm) costs energy; each particle has a **battery** of fixed capacity and can pass a limited amount of energy to a neighbour each time it is activated (an **activation**). The goal is that no particle stays **stressed** (short of energy for its next action) for long, and that the system as a whole keeps acting; we count **rounds** (intervals of time in which every particle is activated at least once). Particles have constant memory and no compass.

ideas.title: Share energy down a forest, and hold back when a particle is stressed
ideas.idea:
1. **Set-up.** The sources are **roots**. Every other particle picks a neighbour that is already in a tree as its *parent*, so the system becomes a forest of trees hanging from the sources.
2. **Signal.** A stressed particle raises a 'stress' flag. A particle with a stressed child raises its flag too, so the signal climbs to the root.
3. **Inhibit.** A root that hears of stress raises an 'inhibit' flag, which spreads down its whole tree: **inhibited** particles stop spending energy on their own actions.
4. **Share.** Roots harvest energy; any particle with enough energy passes some to a child whose battery is not full.
5. **Use.** A particle that is not inhibited and has enough energy performs its next action. Flags are cleared when the stress is gone.
ideas.analysis: Energy flows down the trees like water through pipes, and the inhibit signal stops particles near the source from using everything before it reaches the far ends. [Daymude2021Energy] prove that no particle stays stressed for more than $O(n)$ rounds; without the inhibit step, their simulations show particles staying stressed forever. With a constant number of sources this is optimal, by the next idea. [Weber2023Energy] show how to run any algorithm designed without energy limits on top of this: one that needs $T$ rounds then needs $O(n^2\,T)$ rounds.
ideas.why_it_matters: It was the first model of energy as a limited resource in programmable matter, and the stress/inhibit signals are modelled on how bacterial biofilms share nutrients.

ideas.title: Energy enters only through the sources
ideas.idea: Start with every battery empty and every particle needing a full battery. Then the system needs $n$ full batteries' worth of energy in total. Energy enters only at the $s$ sources, and each source harvests at most a fixed amount per activation. An unkind scheduler activates each source only once per round.
ideas.analysis: So at most a constant times $s$ units of energy enter per round, and filling $n$ batteries takes at least a constant times $n/s$ rounds: $\Omega(n/s)$ [Daymude2021Energy] (Theorem 9). With a constant number of sources this matches the $O(n)$ algorithm; with many sources there is a gap of a factor $s$ between $n/s$ and $n$ that has not been closed.
ideas.why_it_matters: It is a supply argument rather than a distance argument: the bottleneck is how fast energy can enter, not how far it must travel.

glossary.definition: an anonymous computing unit of constant size that occupies one node of the triangular lattice, or two neighbouring nodes while it moves
the infinite graph $G_\Delta$ whose nodes are the corners of a tiling of the plane by equilateral triangles; every node has six neighbours
a point of the triangular lattice; it is empty or occupied by a particle (an expanded particle occupies two)
two nodes are neighbours when an edge of the triangular lattice joins them; two particles are neighbours when they occupy neighbouring nodes
the action in which a particle that occupies one node extends into an empty neighbouring node and then occupies both
the action in which a particle that occupies two nodes withdraws into one of them
one of the $s$ particles that can harvest energy from outside, at most a fixed amount per activation
the energy a particle stores, between 0 and a fixed capacity; every action spends energy from it
one action of a particle chosen by the scheduler: it looks at its neighbourhood, updates its state and performs at most one expansion or contraction
a particle is stressed when its battery holds less energy than its next action costs
a particle is inhibited while its root's inhibit signal is set; it then spends no energy on its own actions and only passes energy on
a source at the top of a tree of particles in which every other particle points to a neighbour, its parent; energy flows from parents to children
an interval of time in which every particle is activated at least once (an asynchronous round); a bound holds for every division of the execution into consecutive rounds

history: Energy distribution was inspired by biofilms [Daymude2021Energy]; the later question was a **general transformation** of energy-agnostic algorithms and its overhead under unfair adversaries [Weber2023Energy].

variants.title: Unfair adversary
variants.summary: Energy can be distributed in $O(n)$ rounds, against an $\Omega(n/s)$ lower bound; any conforming energy-agnostic algorithm becomes energy-constrained with $O(n^2)$ rounds of overhead per action, even under an unfair adversary.

results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorem 8); a self-stabilising spanning forest tolerates crash failures.
Theorem 4: $T_A(n)$ is the running time of the energy-agnostic algorithm. Composes with the concurrency control framework.

variants.notes: No orientation is assumed. Checked against the full texts.

figure.caption: Energy distribution, following [Daymude2021Energy]: numbers are battery levels (capacity 3) and every action costs 1; only the source (amber) harvests energy, 1 per round. The particles form a tree hanging from the source (arrows point to parents); a particle with energy to spare passes 1 to a child whose battery is not full. A particle with an empty battery is stressed (red): it raises a flag that climbs to the root (outlined), the root then inhibits its tree (grey: inhibited particles stop spending energy on their own actions), and energy flows down until the stress is gone; then the flags clear and everyone acts again. One frame per round.
